summary: Describes principles of traffic engineering in IP networks and gives a common basis for developing and evaluating TE capabilities. It was replaced by RFC 9522.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how a network operator keeps traffic flowing well: measure what the network is actually doing, work out where the pressure is, and then change routing, capacity or traffic settings to relieve it. It gives a four-step cycle that repeats, and a way of classifying the tools that do the job.

questions: what are the phases of the traffic engineering process
how do you reduce network congestion
subtitle: A framework for measuring, modelling and steering traffic so IP networks use their capacity well and avoid congestion.

tldr.problem: Networks are built and run to carry traffic, but traffic does not spread itself evenly. Some links fill up while others sit idle, and the network as a whole performs worse than its capacity suggests it could.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines traffic engineering as the measurement, characterisation, modelling and control of Internet traffic, and gives a four-phase process model that repeats: set the policies, measure the network, analyse the result, and optimise by changing routes, capacity or traffic parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3272 was Informational. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9522 and updated by RFC 5462.

facts.label: Traffic oriented performance measures
facts.value: Delay, delay variation, packet loss and throughput

today: RFC 3272 was Informational. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9522 and updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: What Internet Traffic Engineering Is
sections.content:
Internet traffic engineering is defined as that aspect of Internet network engineering dealing with performance evaluation and performance optimization of operational IP networks. It encompasses the application of technology and scientific principles to the measurement, characterization, modeling and control of Internet traffic.

Enhancing the performance of an operational network, at both the traffic and resource levels, is a major objective. This is accomplished by addressing traffic oriented performance requirements while using network resources economically and reliably. The traffic oriented performance measures named are delay, delay variation, packet loss and throughput.

Another objective is reliable network operation. That can be facilitated by mechanisms that enhance network integrity and by policies that emphasize network survivability, which minimizes the vulnerability of the network to outages arising from errors, faults and failures.

The RFC notes that one of the most distinctive functions of Internet traffic engineering is the control and optimization of the routing function, to steer traffic through the network in the most effective way. But it warns against the obvious mistake. Ultimately the performance of the network as seen by end users is what is paramount, and the characteristics visible to end users are the emergent properties of the network. Optimizing the wrong measures may achieve certain local objectives but have disastrous consequences on those emergent properties and therefore on the quality of service perceived by end users.

The optimization work is done through capacity management and traffic management. Capacity management includes capacity planning, routing control and resource management; the resources of particular interest are link bandwidth, buffer space and computational resources. Traffic management includes nodal traffic control functions such as traffic conditioning, queue management and scheduling, and other functions that regulate traffic flow through the network or arbitrate access to network resources between packets or traffic streams.

The control dimension responds at several time scales. Capacity planning operates at very coarse levels, ranging from days to possibly years. Routing control operates at intermediate levels, ranging from milliseconds to days. Packet level processing functions such as rate shaping, queue management and scheduling operate at very fine levels, ranging from picoseconds to milliseconds, responding to the real-time statistical behaviour of traffic. The subsystems of traffic engineering control are capacity augmentation, routing control, traffic control, and resource control, which includes control of service policies at network elements. The inputs to the control system are network state variables, policy variables and decision variables.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic engineering is about the whole network, not one router. The measure that matters is what a user at the end experiences, so a change that helps one link but hurts the network as a whole is a bad change.

sections.title: Scope: Inside One Network
sections.content:
The scope of the document is intra-domain traffic engineering: traffic engineering within a given autonomous system in the Internet. The document discusses concepts pertaining to intra-domain traffic control, including routing control, micro and macro resource allocation, and the control coordination problems that arise consequently.

The document describes and characterizes techniques already in use or in advanced development for Internet traffic engineering, discusses how those techniques fit together, and identifies scenarios in which they are useful.

While it considers various intra-domain approaches, it focuses more on traffic engineering with MPLS. Traffic engineering based upon manipulation of IGP metrics is not addressed in detail; the topic may be addressed by other working group documents.

Although the emphasis is on intra-domain traffic engineering, an overview of the high level considerations pertaining to inter-domain traffic engineering is provided, because inter-domain traffic engineering is crucial to the performance enhancement of the global Internet infrastructure. The reason for the focus is stated early on: Internet traffic engineering is most effective when applied end-to-end, but because a preponderance of Internet traffic tends to be inter-domain, that is, originating in one autonomous system and terminating in another, the document also covers the inter-domain aspect.
sections.plainLanguage: The document stays mostly inside one operator's network, because that is where the measurements and the control are. Where a route crosses into another network, it only summarises the issues.

sections.title: The Problem: Congestion, Capacity and Measurement
sections.content:
Congestion is called out as one of the most significant problems in an operational IP context. A network element is said to be congested if it experiences sustained overload over an interval of time, and congestion almost always results in degradation of service quality to end users.

Congestion control schemes can include demand side policies and supply side policies. Demand side policies may restrict access to congested resources and dynamically regulate demand to alleviate the overload. Supply side policies may expand or augment network capacity to better accommodate the offered traffic, and may also re-allocate network resources by redistributing traffic over the infrastructure. Traffic redistribution and resource re-allocation serve to increase the effective capacity seen by the demand.

The RFC separates the levels at which performance is judged. The system level characteristics of the network are the macro-states, also known as the emergent properties; the resource level characteristics, which restrict attention to individual network resources, are the micro-states. Schemes that optimise at the system level are called macro-TE, and schemes that optimise at the individual resource level are micro-TE. Under certain circumstances the system level performance can be derived from the resource level performance using appropriate rules of composition.

Three classes of problem run through the chapter. One concerns identifying, abstracting, representing and measuring the network features relevant to traffic engineering. Another concerns how to measure and estimate relevant network state parameters: effective traffic engineering relies on a good estimate of the offered traffic load as well as a view of the underlying topology and associated resource constraints, and a network-wide view of the topology is also a must for offline planning. The third concerns how to optimize network performance effectively, which may entail translating solutions into network configurations, and may involve resource management control, routing control, or capacity augmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Overload is the thing to avoid. There are two ways out: turn down the traffic that is causing it, or spread it across more capacity. The RFC also separates the question of whether the whole network is working well from whether one particular link is working well.

sections.title: The Four-Phase Process Model
sections.content:
The process model describes the high level practical aspects of traffic engineering in an operational context, as a sequence of actions a traffic engineer, or a traffic engineering system, must perform to optimize the performance of an operational network. It is a generic model that captures activities common to most methodologies, even though the details of execution differ from network to network, and it may be enacted explicitly or implicitly, by an automaton or by a human.

The model is iterative and has four phases that are repeated continually.

The first phase defines the relevant control policies that govern the operation of the network. These may depend on many factors including the prevailing business model, the network cost structure, the operating constraints, the utility model and the optimization criteria.

The second phase is a feedback mechanism involving the acquisition of measurement data from the operational network. If empirical data is not readily available, synthetic workloads may be used instead, reflecting the prevailing or the expected workload of the network, derived by estimation or extrapolation using prior empirical data, or by mathematical models of traffic characteristics.

The third phase analyses the network state and characterizes the traffic workload. Performance analysis may be proactive, identifying potential problems that do not exist yet but could manifest in the future, or reactive, identifying existing problems, determining their cause through diagnosis, and evaluating alternative approaches to remedy the problem. The analysis may involve investigating the concentration and distribution of traffic across the network, identifying the characteristics of the offered workload, and identifying existing or potential bottlenecks and network pathologies such as ineffective link placement or single points of failure. A traffic matrix may be constructed as part of the analysis.

The fourth phase is performance optimization: a decision process which selects and implements a set of actions from a set of alternatives. Actions may include controlling the offered traffic or its distribution, adding links or increasing link capacity, deploying additional routers and switches, systematically adjusting routing parameters such as IGP metrics and BGP attributes, and adjusting traffic management parameters. Network performance optimization may also involve starting a network planning process to improve the architecture, design, capacity, technology and configuration of network elements to accommodate growth.
sections.plainLanguage: The cycle is: decide what you want, measure what is happening, work out what is wrong, change something, and start again.

sections.title: A Taxonomy of Traffic Engineering Systems
sections.content:
The document presents a short taxonomy of traffic engineering systems, built from seven pairs of classifications.

Time-dependent, state-dependent or event-dependent. In time-dependent TE, historical information based on periodic variations in traffic, such as time of day, is used to pre-program routing plans; these plans typically change on a relatively long time scale. State-dependent TE adapts routing plans based on the current state of the network, which provides information about variations in actual traffic that could not be predicted from history. Event-dependent methods are adaptive and distributed, and typically use learning models to find good paths.

Offline or online. Traffic engineering requires the computation of routing plans. Offline computation suits scenarios where plans need not be executed in real time, and is also used for extensive searches over multi-dimensional solution spaces. Online computation is required when plans must adapt to changing network conditions, and is geared toward simpler and faster calculations to select routes, fine-tune resource allocations and balance load.

Centralized or distributed. Centralized control has a central authority that determines routing plans on behalf of each router, collecting network state information periodically and returning routing information; the routing update cycle is a critical parameter. Distributed control has each router select routes autonomously based on its own view of the network state, obtained by probing or by periodic distribution of link state advertisements.

Local or global. Local information pertains to the state of a portion of the domain, such as the bandwidth and packet loss rate of a particular path. Global information pertains to the state of the entire domain, such as a global traffic matrix, and is typically required with centralized control.

Prescriptive or descriptive. Prescriptive traffic engineering evaluates alternatives and recommends a course of action, and can be corrective, addressing an existing or predicted anomaly, or perfective, improving performance even when no anomalies are evident. Descriptive traffic engineering characterizes the state of the network and assesses the impact of various policies without recommending any particular course of action.

Open-loop or closed-loop. Open-loop control does not use feedback information from the current network state. Closed-loop control uses it, in the form of historical information or current measurement.

Tactical or strategic. Tactical traffic engineering addresses specific performance problems, such as hot-spots, from a tactical perspective, without consideration of overall strategic imperatives; without proper planning and insights it tends to be ad hoc. Strategic traffic engineering approaches the problem from a more organized and systematic perspective, taking into consideration the immediate and longer term consequences of specific policies and actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Any traffic engineering system can be placed on seven scales, from how quickly it reacts to whether one person or a whole team decides, and each choice has a different cost and benefit.

sections.title: What a Traffic Engineering System Should Provide
sections.content:
The recommendations section is divided into functional recommendations, which describe the functions a traffic engineering system should perform, and non-functional recommendations, which relate to quality attributes or state characteristics and may contain conflicting assertions and be difficult to quantify precisely.

The generic non-functional recommendations are usability, automation, scalability, stability, visibility, simplicity, efficiency, reliability, correctness, maintainability, extensibility, interoperability and security. In a given context some may be critical and others optional, so prioritization may be required to tailor the system to an operational environment.

Several are elaborated. Automation: whenever feasible, a traffic engineering system should automate as many traffic engineering functions as possible to minimize human effort, and this is particularly imperative in large scale public networks because of the high cost of the human aspects of network operations and the high risk of network problems caused by human errors. Scalability: a TE system should remain functional as the network expands in the number of routers and links and in traffic volume, should not adversely impair other functions and processes in a network element, and should not consume too much network resources when collecting and distributing state information. Stability: state-dependent methodologies typically mandate a tradeoff between responsiveness and stability, and it is strongly recommended that where such a tradeoff is warranted the tradeoff be made in favour of stability, especially in public IP backbone networks. Visibility: mechanisms should exist to collect statistics from the network and analyse them, and derived statistics such as traffic matrices, link utilization, latency and packet loss can be used as indicators of prevailing network conditions. Simplicity: a TE system should be as simple as possible, and complexities in the algorithms should be hidden as much as possible from the network administrator. Interoperability: systems and their components should be developed with open standards based interfaces to allow interoperation with other systems and components.

The document also notes that it introduces no new security issues of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: When a system reacts to what it measures, it can chase its own tail. The RFC's advice is to favour a steady network over a fast-reacting one when the choice has to be made.

viz.caption: THE TIME SCALES OF THE CONTROL FUNCTIONS (RFC 3272)
THE FOUR PHASES OF THE PROCESS MODEL

items.title: 1. Define policies
items.text: Set the policies that govern the network: business model, cost structure, operating constraints and optimization criteria.

items.title: 2. Measure
items.text: Collect measurement data from the operational network, or use synthetic workloads if empirical data is not available.

items.title: 3. Analyse
items.text: Characterize the network state and the traffic workload; find existing or potential bottlenecks and network pathologies.

items.title: 4. Optimize
items.text: Select and implement actions: control the offered traffic or its distribution, add links or capacity, tune routing parameters.

items.title: Time, state or event
items.text: Time-dependent uses history and forecasts; state-dependent uses the current network state; event-dependent learns from past events.

items.title: Offline or online
items.text: Offline computation suits plans that need not run in real time; online computation adapts to changing conditions.

items.title: Centralized or distributed
items.text: A central authority computes the plans, or each router decides on its own from its view of the network.

items.title: Local or global
items.text: Algorithms may need the state of part of the domain or of the whole of it.

items.title: Prescriptive or descriptive
items.text: Prescriptive recommends an action; descriptive characterizes the network without recommending one.

items.title: Open-loop or closed-loop
items.text: Open-loop control ignores feedback from the network; closed-loop control uses it.

items.title: Tactical or strategic
items.text: Tactical fixes a specific problem now; strategic considers the longer term consequences.
